2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate-to-high concern: 27 camps from the initial May 2010 random sample closed before July 2010 (all lacking NGO management, requiring replacement from the 7 July DTM), 14 of 113 visited camps no longer existed leaving 99 analysed camps (pp. S3–S4), 8 additional camps closed by the January 2011 follow-up (pp. S13–S14), and within the 99 analysed camps item missingness was substantial for verified water availability (71/99 complete; 28.3% missing) and toilet cleaning frequency (50/63 camps with toilets; 20.6% missing; Table 1, p. S6).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: NGO camp management was non-randomly distributed across central vs. peripheral municipalities (45.3% vs. 14.3%, p=0.004) and public vs. private land (47.8% vs. 27.4%, p=0.068; p. S12). Despite referencing multivariate analyses in the abstract, statistical testing relied solely on unadjusted two-way and three-way chi-square contingency tables (dropping Cite Soleil in Table 5 due to small cell counts), with no multivariable regression and no neighbourhood or household socioeconomic status controls (pp. S4–S5, S9–S13).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate (adequate-to-weak): International humanitarian/human-rights standards (UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement, UNGA Resolution 64/292, Sphere Minimum Standards; p. S2) frame the inquiry, while domestic legal/institutional exposures—public vs. private land tenure ('Met te a', collapsing churches and private schools into private ownership; p. S5), formal IOM DTM camp-manager registration ('Gen ONG kap dirije kan'), municipal boundaries, 'red zone' security designations, and DINEPA's Cite Soleil mandate and November 2011 water-trucking decree (pp. S14, S16, S18)—are measured through coarse survey/administrative indicators and qualitative interviews without formal title or statutory verification.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Camp outcomes benefited from direct researcher toilet counts, researcher observation of water provision, two-informant corroboration of cleaning frequency, and quality-control revisits by a second assistant and an author across 49 camps (pp. S4–S5). However, binary presence measures did not assess water potability/chlorination (p. S14) or actual clinic staffing/supplies (e.g., an empty UNICEF clinic tent in Carradeux counted as a clinic; p. S8), land tenure collapsed churches with private landowners (p. S5), and IOM DTM listing of NGO camp managers omitted active NGOs that refused database listing due to perceived legal liability (p. S17).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate (adequate): WASH and health service presence was operationalized via direct field observation and corroborated structured survey items across 99 camps—confirming water availability, counting physical toilets relative to IOM DTM camp population, verifying toilet cleaning frequency (1–2 days vs. >=3 days) with at least two informants, and recording clinic presence—backed by duplicate quality-control site visits (pp. S4–S5). Limitations include unmeasured water quality/quantity per capita and clinic functionality, plus 28.3% unverified/missing water observations (p. S6, S8, S14).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol is cited. Endnote 5 (p. S22) notes that three-way stratified analyses (Tables 5–6) were restricted post hoc to measures statistically significantly related to both independent variables. Minor internal reporting discrepancies appear between the abstract (108 camps and 168 interviews; p. S1) and Methods (113 visited / 99 analysed camps and 57 agency interviews plus camp survey interviews; pp. S3–S4), as well as between reported chi-square sample sizes in text and table denominators (N=71 vs. 95 on p. S9; N=88 vs. 50 on p. S11).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate concern: Quantitative sampling used a systematic random sample (every 8th camp) from the 841 metro Port-au-Prince camps in the 3 May 2010 IOM DTM, adding every 32nd camp from the 7 July DTM to replace 27 closed camps (p. S3; Annexe 2, p. S21). Because closed camps had no NGO managers, NGO-managed camps were overrepresented in the sample (33% vs. 20.8%–22% in DTM; pp. S3, S8, S21). Qualitative interviews (n=57 agency/government staff; 9 non-respondents) used purposive/cluster-meeting sampling (p. S3), while selection of quoted camp leaders/residents is minimally specified.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Schuller and Levey (2014) present a primary mixed-methods investigation of WASH and clinic service gaps in Port-au-Prince metropolitan IDP camps following the January 2010 Haiti earthquake and October 2010 cholera outbreak. Appraised with the MMAT (2018) using the Quantitative non-randomized (analytic cross-sectional) block (3.1–3.5), the study's main strengths are its probability sampling frame drawn systematically from the IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix (Annexe 2), direct researcher field observation and duplicate quality-control revisits for physical toilet counts and water availability (p. S4), trilingual semi-structured interviews with 57 humanitarian and government officials alongside camp-level testimonies (p. S3), and strong substantive integration of quantitative patterns with qualitative institutional explanations (5.1–5.4 all 'Yes'). However, per MMAT 2018 guidance that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component, overall methodological concern is moderate-to-high: verified water outcome data were missing for 28.3% of analysed camps (71/99; item 3.3 'No'), statistical analyses relied on unadjusted two-way and selected three-way chi-square crosstabs without multivariable confounding control or socioeconomic covariates despite strong non-random selection of NGOs into central and public-land camps (item 3.4 'No'), pre-survey closure of unmanaged camps inflated the sample share of NGO-managed camps (33% vs. 20.8%–22% in DTM), minor statistical/sample reporting inconsistencies appear in the text (pp. S1, S3–S4, S9, S11), and qualitative coding and researcher reflexivity (including author advocacy in a studied camp; p. S7) are minimally detailed (item 1.3 'Can't tell'; item 5.5 'No').
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (MMAT narrative judgment; bounded by weakest component: strong probability frame and mixed-methods integration, but 28.3% missing water outcome data, unadjusted bivariate/three-way confounding, and limited qualitative coding/reflexivity transparency)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Mixed-methods primary study combining a systematic random-sample analytical cross-sectional survey and direct observational audit of 99 IDP camps in July–August 2010 (plus a January 2011 repeat survey of 83–94 camps) with 57 in-person semi-structured qualitative interviews of IOM, Haitian government, and international NGO staff and qualitative camp resident/committee interviews

raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper explicitly designs and reports a primary mixed-methods empirical study integrating quantitative camp-level survey/observation data (analysed via bivariate and three-way contingency tables comparing WASH outcomes across NGO camp management, municipality, and public/private land tenure, plus pre/post cholera follow-up) with qualitative semi-structured interviews and ethnographic site visits. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT is the mandatory instrument for primary studies combining qualitative and quantitative empirical components, with Quantitative block 3.1–3.5 (non-randomized / analytical cross-sectional) matching the exposure-outcome associative camp comparisons.
